opening.headline: When a customer requests security certification and control documentation, we learn how to distinguish which materials are where, and whether they are the provider's responsibility or ours.
body: Large customers require documentation regarding certification status, data protection controls, and access management methods during the adoption review. At this point, the certification materials provided by the vendor mix with our own configured settings, making it difficult to determine which side is responsible. If inappropriate materials are selected or if configurations are incomplete, the review process becomes prolonged.

In this class, we first divide the responsibilities between the provider and the customer using a shared responsibility model. We then examine how the Trust Center and security documentation are structured, what roles SSO and SCIM play in enterprise applications, and illustrate with examples how to respond to customer audit requests with specific documentation.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of enterprise app security and the Trust Center.
In the shared responsibility model, the responsibility of the provider and the responsibility of the customer can be distinguished.

screens.title: The customer requires security certification and control documentation.
screens.lead: First, review the list of requests received during the introduction review. The diagram illustrates how requests are assigned between the provider's responsibility and the customer's responsibility.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the customer's security requirements divided into provider responsibility area and customer responsibility area, each leading to different sources of information.
labels: Procedure for removing terminated user accounts
Provider Responsibility: Authentication and Infrastructure Control

paragraphs: This is a hypothetical scenario. A large enterprise customer requires documentation during the AI service adoption review, specifying four areas: the supplier's certification status, data protection controls, access management approach, and how retired accounts are removed.

The issue is that these four elements do not originate from a single source. The certification report is held by the provider, while access management and account deactivation depend on our configured settings. If these are combined, it becomes difficult to determine which party is responsible.

Sending incorrect documentation can prolong the review process. For example, sending a certification report for a product we do not use, or sending only the supplier's certification while omitting the configuration settings that the customer must set up, will result in follow-up questions.

callout.label: Questions to be answered in this class
callout.text: Where is a given piece of data located, and what is the provider's responsibility versus our responsibility?

screens.outro: First, let's think about our experiences so far.

screens.title: Recall the experience of delivering vendor security materials to customers.
screens.lead: First, think through each question on your own before selecting an answer. The instructor's thoughts will then be organized and presented. No answers are submitted.

items.prompt: Have you ever delivered vendor certification reports and certificates to customers?
items.answer: This material is a result proven by the provider through external audit. It is not something we can create; it must be received through procedures defined by the provider, and the core focus is to verify that it aligns with our products and scope.

items.prompt: Where did you find the security control documentation or configuration guide?
items.answer: This information is often scattered across the provider's help center or documentation site. This material explains how control works but does not prove that we have configured it.

items.prompt: Have we ever verified access controls that we have directly configured?
items.answer: SSO configuration, user provisioning method, and logging settings are areas configured by the customer. We need to prepare materials that describe the configured settings and the current status.

items.prompt: Did you indicate whose responsibility it is for each piece of data before delivering it?
items.answer: If even one line indicating responsibility is displayed, the customer clearly understands how to read the material. By first understanding the shared responsibility model, classification becomes easier, and then we examine that model on the next screen.

screens.outro: Now let's verify the fundamental framework for sharing responsibilities.

screens.title: Shared Responsibility Model: Cloud Security and Security Within the Cloud
screens.lead: Compare the provider's responsible area and the customer's responsible area by alternately selecting two states. Pay attention to the fact that the extent of the customer's responsibility varies depending on the service type.

visual.alt: A two-layer diagram with the customer responsibility area on top and the provider responsibility area below.
labels: Customer Responsibility: Security within the Cloud
Boundaries move depending on service type

states.label: Cloud Security: Provider Responsibility
states.body: In the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, the provider protects the infrastructure on which the service runs. This infrastructure consists of hardware, software, networks, and facilities. In AI services, authentication and infrastructure controls fall within this layer, and customers verify these through the provider's authentication reports and certificates. Since customers cannot directly modify this area, it is appropriate for the provider to request third-party verified evidence.

states.label: Security within the Cloud: Customer Responsibility
states.body: The customer is responsible for their data, applications, access configurations, and encryption choices. The extent of this responsibility varies depending on the type of service selected. For example, with IaaS services like EC2, the customer is responsible for operations such as OS patching and firewall configuration. In contrast, with abstracted services like S3, the provider manages the infrastructure layer, and the customer focuses on data and permission settings. The same principle applies to AI services. Responsibilities such as SSO, user provisioning, and logging are not handled by the provider and remain the customer's responsibility. By dividing customer inquiries into these two layers, clear paths to answers become evident.

screens.outro: Since responsibilities have been assigned, we will examine the location where materials pertaining to the provider's responsibility area are gathered.

screens.title: Composition of the Trust Center and Security and Compliance Documentation
screens.lead: When you select the diagram number marker, you can view detailed descriptions of the components related to the Trust Center and associated documentation.

visual.alt: Diagram showing the layout of the Trust Center page. It includes an upper access request button, scope matrix, data list, and a collection of help center links.

markers.label: Access Request
markers.title: Sensitive documents are viewed after request.
markers.body: The Anthropic Trust Center collects compliance materials and allows users to request documentation by submitting a request form. To view sensitive documents, users must click the "Access Request" button and complete the request form. Documents must not be shared arbitrarily without going through the request process.

markers.label: Scope Matrix
markers.title: View certification status by product at a glance
markers.body: The scope matrix displays certification status such as SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, CSA STAR, HIPAA, and NIST 800-171 per product. Rows are categorized by API, Enterprise, Team, and Cloud Partner. For example, Team shows no HIPAA coverage. Users must read the row corresponding to the product they are using.

markers.label: Partner Management Indicator
markers.title: Responsibility varies depending on the hosting environment.
markers.body: Even with the same model, certain items such as HIPAA compliance may be displayed under the partner management section when going through Amazon Bedrock or Vertex AI. Since these items require adherence to the documentation of the respective cloud partner, they must be read on a product-and-hosting-environment basis.

markers.label: material type
markers.title: Types of documents that can be received
markers.body: The materials include SOC 2 reports, ISO certificates and compliance declarations, HIPAA reports and implementation guides, NIST certificates, and subsidiary processor information as well as FAQ. Customers must select the appropriate documentation based on the required certifications.

markers.label: Help Center Collection
markers.title: The usage of control is described in a separate document.
markers.body: The security and compliance collection in Claude's Help Center bundles documents such as data processors versus administrators, data deletion, export, data retention, IP allow lists, and audit logs. Other providers offer similar content. Google provides compliance certification and security controls in a table format, while AWS offers a separate page for its shared responsibility model.

screens.outro: Now that we know the location of the provider's data, let's examine the access controls that the customer needs to configure directly.

screens.title: Enterprise App Security: SSO and SCIM
screens.lead: Compare Claude's user provisioning mode in the table. Pay attention to the differences in when users are created and how they are removed.

data.caption: Comparison of Claude User Provisioning Modes
rows: Automatically generated when the assigned user first logs in to the IdP app
Manual removal required; even after releasing the IdP assignment, the member list and seats remain.
When a user belonging to a mapped group logs in, the highest-privilege role is created for them.
Mostly passive; removed upon next login in all mapping groups where it is missing
Generate automatically without waiting for login, based on IdP assignment
Removed in IdP app will be automatically removed
Automatically generated with role based on mapped group
Group access is automatically revoked and removed, and role changes are automatically reflected.
data.notes: SSO is the authentication method for login, while SCIM is provisioning that synchronizes users and groups between the IdP. The two can be configured independently, but JIT or SCIM must be set up after SSO and domain authentication are completed. OpenAI also provides SCIM, available at the tenant level, ChatGPT workspace level, and API organization level, with availability varying by plan. In ChatGPT Enterprise, workspace settings delegate management of members, roles, seats, and identity controls to administrators. These settings fall under the customer's responsibility, and the provider does not handle them; whether a customer's former accounts are immediately removed depends on which mode is being used.

screens.outro: Now, let's move on to an example of matching these materials to actual customer requests.

screens.title: Explanation: Selecting materials to convey in customer satisfaction response scenarios
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the scenario step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Verify the requested items
steps.body: The customer requested four items: SOC 2 report, access management approach, offboarding account removal procedure, and log retention status. Based on the two-layer responsibility model of shared responsibility, we first identify the responsible parties for each item.

steps.title: The SOC 2 report is obtained from the Trust Center.
steps.body: The SOC 2 report and certificate are within the responsibility of the provider. Access to them should be requested through the Trust Center. After receiving them, we verify that the scope of the report aligns with the products we use and the hosting environment.

steps.title: Access management is answered by our configuration.
steps.body: Access management is within our responsibility area. We will prepare documentation explaining how SSO is configured, whether user provisioning is invite-only, JIT, or SCIM.

steps.title: Employee removal is explained depending on the mode.
steps.body: If SCIM is used, it is explained that accounts are automatically removed when allocation is revoked in the IdP. If JIT is used, it is explained that members remain in the member list even after allocation is revoked in the IdP, requiring a manual removal process, and this process is also provided.

steps.title: Log retention is determined by the current configuration.
steps.body: Log retention is determined by the audit logs and Compliance API configuration status. It explicitly reflects the current configuration regarding who can export logs and how long they are retained. If no configuration has been set, it clearly states this fact along with the planned configuration.

steps.title: Lists each responsible party individually.
steps.body: For each response, indicate in one line which part is the responsibility of the provider and which part is our responsibility. Customers can immediately see this indication and know exactly which evidence to verify with whom.

screens.outro: Next, we will examine a common vulnerability in thank-you responses.

screens.title: Explanation: Common vulnerabilities in thank-you response scenarios
screens.lead: Expand by selecting each item to see common weaknesses and the recommended responses preferred by instructors. Read through considering whether your organization has any of these vulnerabilities.

items.title: Gap 1: Sending reports from products with different authentication scopes
items.body: Compliance status varies by product and hosting environment. Even among the same provider, the scope differs—for example, Team products do not include HIPAA coverage as with other offerings. The scope should be confirmed at the product and hosting environment level used by the customer, and it should be reviewed again before submitting the report.

items.title: Gap 2: Customer responsibility is not yet defined
items.body: Providing only vendor authentication does not eliminate the customer's configuration burden. Auditors point out issues when vendor authentication is presented without SSO, provisioning, or logging configuration. Verify the configuration status prior to review.

items.title: Gap 3: Confusing responsibility for partner's transit environment
items.body: When using a model through Amazon Bedrock or Vertex AI, certain items are displayed in the partner management section. For these items, the model provider must respond with documentation and verification from the cloud partner, not the model provider itself.

items.title: Gap 4: Sharing sensitive documents without access requests
items.body: Documents classified as sensitive in the Trust Center are accessible only after an access request is processed. When delivering received documents to customers, the provider adheres to the conditions specified by the provider and does not redistribute them at will. By pre-designating internal personnel and authorized individuals with viewing permissions, responses to access requests can be handled more promptly.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize the previous content into a single reference point.

screens.title: Summary: Authentication is the provider's responsibility, while configuration is the customer's responsibility.
screens.lead: Summarize the content discussed so far. Please read the following paragraphs in sequence.

paragraphs: The shared responsibility model divides the responsibilities such that the provider is accountable for infrastructure and authentication, while the customer is responsible for data and access controls. By separating the customer's security requirements into these two layers, it becomes clear where data is stored.

The Trust Center is a repository that consolidates certification status by product and hosting environment, as well as security documentation. Sensitive documents must be accessed upon request and reviewed to ensure the scope of the received reports aligns with the products we are using. SSO handles authentication, while SCIM manages the user lifecycle; both must be configured directly by the customer.

Response to inquiries should distinguish between the source and the responsible party for each item. Provider authentication is answered based on the provider's input, while customer configurations are responded to based on our current setup, with a single line indicating which side is responsible. Establishing this habit reduces the duration of reviews and allows potential gaps in configuration to be identified before the review process begins.

glossary.def: This is a website that aggregates the provider's certification status, security documentation, and sub-processor information to receive access requests.
This is documentation that proves the provider's controls through external audits, similar to SOC 2, ISO certificates, and HIPAA reports.
The provider is responsible for the security of the service infrastructure, while the customer is responsible for the security of data and configurations.
SSO is a login authentication method, and SCIM is provisioning that synchronizes the IdP with users and groups.

misconceptions.myth: If the provider authentication is available, our configuration is unnecessary.
misconceptions.fact: Access management and logging are the customer's responsibility. Provider authentication only proves control within the provider's domain and does not substitute for the customer's configuration responsibilities.

misconceptions.myth: Enabling SSO automatically removes the account.
misconceptions.fact: SSO is for login authentication, while automated removal depends on provisioning settings such as SCIM. In JIT, even after revoking IdP assignments, members remain in the member list.

misconceptions.myth: The authentication status is the same regardless of the product.
misconceptions.fact: The scope varies by product and hosting environment. Team does not fall under HIPAA coverage, while Bedrock or Vertex-based services have certain items within the partner management area.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Authentication is the provider's responsibility, and configuration is the customer's responsibility.
The Trust Center gathers certification status by product and hosting environment, along with security documentation.
SSO handles authentication, while SCIM manages the user lifecycle, and customers must configure it themselves.
Thank-you responses are separated by item, specifying both the source and the responsible party.

closing.reflection: What is the scope of our responsibility, and what has not yet been defined?

title: Enterprise app security and Trust Centers

checks.q: The customer asks whether departing user accounts are immediately deleted. Which explanation is appropriate based on provisioning mode?
options: JIT automatically removes users when the IdP assignment is revoked.
SCIM creates and deletes users based on IdP assignment without waiting for login.
SSO is set up, user synchronization and removal are also handled.
The invite-only mode synchronizes automatically with the IdP.
checks.explain: SSO is authentication, and SCIM is provisioning that synchronizes users and groups between the IdP. SCIM automatically removes accounts upon deassignment, whereas JIT requires manual removal.

wrong.0: JIT creates an account during the first login, but removal is manual.
wrong.2: SSO and SCIM are independent; user lifecycle synchronization cannot be achieved solely through SSO.
wrong.3: Invitation-only mode manages access so that only users invited by administrators can enter, and automatic synchronization is not enabled.
